In D, Larry has properly made Dr. Moe an independent defendant on an independent claim. He has not ‘‘stacked’’ anything, because Dr. Moe owes him a separate duty of care, to treat him properly. If he has breached that duty, he is independently liable for his negligent treatment. Since Larry’s claim against Moe does not meet the amount requirement, it cannot be brought in federal court. In C, Larry has properly made both Curly and Moe defendants for his damages from the accident. But he has not sought more than $75,000.01 in damages from either, since, as the question indicates, one or the other (or both) may have been at fault, and he would only collect from the one at fault. He hasn’t stacked anything; he’s simply sued the appropriate parties for his harm. But since he seeks less than the required amount against each, the case cannot be brought in federal court. In B, the plaintiff’s claim clearly does not meet the amount requirement. But what about Curly’s counterclaim? It arises out of the same underlying accident as the plaintiff’s claim, so it is a ‘‘compulsory’’ counterclaim under Fed. R. Civ. P. 13(g). If it is compulsory, it can be brought in federal court even though it does not meet the amount requirement. But is it compulsory? I would think so, since it arises out of the same transaction or occurrence as the plaintiff’s claim. If it is compulsory, the court would have supplemental jurisdiction over it, even though it does not meet the amount requirement. So B is a proper diversity case. A is also a proper diversity case. It’s a little tricky, but here the plaintiffs have stacked their claims. Both suffered harm from the accident, and both sue the sole defendant for their individual losses. Since Larry’s claim does not meet the amount requirement, he has properly added Moe as a plaintiff, to bring the total amount in controversy up to the required level. The defendants cannot object to this, since they are not diverse from either plaintiff. So the answer is B. However, there is a nice argument that the counterclaim in B is not compulsory. Rule 13(g) provides that, if you have a claim against an opposing party that arises out of the same transaction or occurrence as a claim you asserted against that party in the action, you must assert it as a counterclaim. Here, Curly’s claim arises out of the same accident as Larry’s. But he didn’t assert it as a counterclaim; instead, he asserted a crossclaim against Moe. The argument for nonfinality is that, since Moe is not a party to Larry’s claim, Curly’s claim against Moe does not meet the standard for a compulsory counterclaim. This is a clever argument, but I don’t think it will prevail. The point of the compulsory counterclaim rule is to force a party to assert all claims he has against an opposing party, so that they can all be litigated in the first action. Here, Curly’s claim against Moe does arise out of the same transaction as Larry’s claim against Curly. If Curly leaves it out, and the jury finds Larry’s damages to be less than $75,000, he will be able to bring it later in a separate action. That should not be allowed, since the same accident gave rise to his claim against Moe as to Larry. So I think the court would hold that the counterclaim is compulsory, and therefore proper under federal jurisdiction rules.
[/THINK]

This is a nice example, because it requires you to focus on the basic test for domicile, and to sort through a lot of facts to apply it. The facts suggest that Filbert has been all over the map. But the key to his domicile is to look back in time to a point where he was both physically present in a state and intended to remain there indefinitely. The first place he fit that description is Illinois. He lived there, and went to Nebraska with the intent to return. So, Illinois was his domicile when he went to Nebraska. But what about Nebraska? He went there with the intent to leave, so he never established a Nebraska domicile. D suggests that he is domiciled in Nebraska, because he lives there now and has no plans to return to Illinois. But that’s not the test: You must both reside in the state and have an open-ended intent to remain there. Filbert’s stay in Nebraska lacks the necessary intent. So, Nebraska is not his domicile. How about Colorado? He was there, and at one point intended to go back and live there. But that isn’t the test either. The test is not ‘‘state in which you once intended to live.’’ It is, ‘‘state in which you decided to live there and did live there.’’ Filbert never actually lived in Colorado, so it can’t be his domicile. That brings us to B, which is the winner. Illinois is his domicile because it is the last state in which he both lived and had an open-ended intent to remain there.
[/THINK]

This question illustrates a common situation: The plaintiff files a suit in federal court, the defendant answers and proceeds to litigate in the federal court, and then later moves to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. This is permissible under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(2), which provides that ‘‘the determination of the court that it has no jurisdiction over the case shall be made as soon as made appearing.’’ So, Taney can raise the objection to jurisdiction at this point, even though he did not assert it at the outset of the case. The question, then, is, what should the court do when it appears that it might lack subject matter jurisdiction over the case? One possibility is that the court should dismiss the case if it lacks ‘‘arising under’’ jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §1332(a), even if it has jurisdiction under the Article III, §2 ‘‘arising under’’ test. This is the position taken by A. This is a nice idea, since it would promote uniformity in the interpretation of §1332(a) (as opposed to Article III, §2), but it has not been accepted by the courts. Instead, they have taken the position that, if the case is within the constitutional grant of jurisdiction in Article III, §2, the court has the power to hear it, even if it does not fall within the statutory grant in §1332(a). The very language of §1332(a) refutes the argument for A. Section 1332(a) grants the federal district courts the jurisdiction conferred by Article III, §2, and ‘‘such special jurisdiction as they may be authorized by law to exercise.’’ So, the district courts have the jurisdiction granted in Article III, §2, even if they are not authorized to hear a case by §1332(a). In addition, the cases have rejected the argument for A. D’Urville v. D’Urville, 216 F.2d 636 (1st Cir. 1950); 13C Wright, Miller & Cooper §3521, pp. 101-102. If the case is proper under the Article III test, the court has the constitutional power to hear it, even if it does not satisfy §1332(a). B reflects this position. If the court has jurisdiction under the Article III, §2 ‘‘arising under’’ test, it has the power to hear the case, even if the plaintiff’s claim does not ‘‘arise under’’ federal law within the meaning of §1332(a). C is also wrong. Even if the case is within the constitutional grant of jurisdiction, the court must still dismiss if it appears that there is no statutory grant of jurisdiction. But this one isn’t lacking statutory jurisdiction, since 28 U.S.C. §1331 confers jurisdiction on federal district courts to hear cases arising under federal law (as long as the amount in controversy is over $75,000, or diversity jurisdiction is proper). And §1331 (the federal ‘‘general jurisdiction’’ statute) is authorized by the federal ‘‘federal question’’ category in Article III, §2. So, if the case meets the constitutional test for an ‘‘arising under’’ case, and is authorized by §1331, the court has both constitutional and statutory authority to hear it. D is wrong, because there is a statutory grant of jurisdiction in §1331, just as there is a constitutional grant in Article III, §2. So, the court need not rely on inferring a grant of jurisdiction from the fact that the parties consent to the court’s jurisdiction. They can’t confer jurisdiction on the court by consent, even if the case does not satisfy the statutory grant. The court must have a statutory grant of jurisdiction as well as a constitutional one. So, B is the best answer. If the case meets the constitutional test for an ‘‘arising under’’ case, the court has the power to hear it, even if the plaintiff’s claim does not ‘‘arise under’’ federal law within the meaning of §1332(a).
[/THINK]
B

[THINK]
The key to this question is the basic point that the federal courts can only hear cases within the constitutional limits on their jurisdiction. Here, the case was brought in state court. The state court heard and decided it. The loser then sought review in the United States Supreme Court. Can the Supreme Court hear the case? Only if it is within the reach of one of the articles of the Constitution, which grant jurisdiction to the federal courts. Article III, §2, which creates federal ‘‘arising under’’ jurisdiction, is not satisfied, because this is a case between private parties, not the federal government, and no federal statute or other federal ingredient is actually involved in the case. The Mottleys’ argument based on the Fifth Amendment is a state law argument, not a federal one. The federal constitution is a limit on the power of government to make the law, not a source of the law. The state courts, like the federal courts, must enforce the constraints of the federal constitution on the exercise of governmental power. But when they do, they are not applying federal law, they are applying state law. The state courts, like all courts, must refuse to enforce a state statute that violates the federal constitution. But the state court’s power to do so flows from the state constitution, not the federal. The state courts are not federal courts, and their authority to hear cases does not come from Article III of the federal constitution. It comes from the constitution of the state in which they sit. Thus, the fact that the Mottleys relied on the federal constitution to defend their case does not make it a case ‘‘arising under’’ the constitution. It’s a state law case, and the federal courts cannot hear or review it. A is the right answer. Note that this does not mean that the federal courts will never hear a case involving a claim that a state statute is invalid because it violates the federal constitution. They will, if the case is brought in federal court, and the defendant asserts the unconstitutionality of the statute as a defense. But if the case is brought in federal court, it must be within the constitutional limits on federal court jurisdiction. If it is, the federal court will hear and determine all defenses in the case, including constitutional defenses. But if the case is not within the constitutional limits on federal court jurisdiction, it cannot be heard in federal court, even if the plaintiff would like it heard there, and even if the defendant has a defense to it that involves a federal question.
[/THINK]
A

[THINK]
Let’s start with D. It is true that the case is within the federal diversity jurisdiction, but that doesn’t mean it is properly removed. Removal requires not only that the federal court would have jurisdiction, but also compliance with the procedural requirements in §1446. One of those is the requirement that all defendants join in or consent to removal. That hasn’t been done here. Ivens didn’t join in the notice of removal, and the question indicates that he didn’t consent to it either. B is partly right. Since Ivens did not join in the notice of removal, it is incomplete. But that doesn’t mean the case can’t be removed. It means that Ivens may object to removal, and did. The question then becomes, is his objection timely? It is not. Section 1447(c) provides that objections to removal, other than lack of subject matter jurisdiction, must be raised within thirty days after removal. Ivens’s motion is too late. A is also a loser. Although the amount-in-controversy objection may be raised anytime, that doesn’t mean that it is proper here. The amount-in-controversy requirement is met: Tyrgyz seeks $120,000 against the two doctors. A party meets the amount requirement by demanding that amount from the defendants collectively, even if he doesn’t specify how much he demands from each. See, e.g., Garside v. Osceola Ref. Co., 248 U.S. 80 (1918). So, C is the best answer. The case is properly within the federal court’s jurisdiction, and Ivens’s objection has been waived by the untimely motion to remand.
[/THINK]
C

[THINK]
This question is a bit a twist on the scenario in the previous question. Here, the plaintiff initially files suit in state court. The defendant stays there, litigating on the merits, and then removes after Rasmussen adds a federal claim to the case. The first answer suggests that this is all right, because the case became removable when the federal claim was added. But this doesn’t quite cut the mustard. Removal must be based on the case as it is at the time of removal. There is a reason for this basic rule: A plaintiff who files in state court should not have to guess whether the defendant will seek federal court. If the case is properly removed, the plaintiff has an interest in knowing that at the time of filing. If the case is not a proper diversity case, and there is no federal ingredient, the plaintiff has the right to assume that the defendant will litigate in state court. If the defendant’s options are not clear at the time of filing, the defendant will have to choose between removing immediately or staying in state court. If she stays, and the case later becomes removable, too bad; the removal option is lost. A is wrong here, because at the time of removal the case is a hybrid of state and federal claims—one arising under federal law, the other arising under state law. As in the last question, the state law claim is not a proper diversity claim, since Apex, the sole defendant, is a citizen of the forum state. So D is right; the state breach of contract claim may not be removed. But what about the federal claim? Is it removable? I suppose an argument could be made that, since it arises under federal law, it is a separate suit that may be removed. But this seems like overkill, and is not the usual approach to this scenario. Generally, when a plaintiff adds a federal claim to a case, the case is viewed as a single ‘‘case or controversy’’ (as §1441(a) puts it) between the parties, not as separate suits. See, e.g., Galt v. Liberty Mountain, Inc., 827 F. Supp. 1531, 1533 (M.D. Fla. 1993). And, if it is a single case or controversy, it is a case that arises under state law, since the state law claim is jurisdictionally predominant. So I think the better view is that the case is not properly removed. C is also wrong. It suggests that Rasmussen should have removed the case initially. But the case was not removable initially, since it was a state law claim and there was no diversity jurisdiction. So Rasmussen was entitled to file in state court, and the case would have remained there, had Rasmussen not voluntarily injected a federal ingredient into it. Thus, B is wrong too. There is no problem with removing a case in which there is an in-state defendant, as long as the standards for removal are met. Here, they are not met, because the case isn’t a proper diversity case, and isn’t based on federal law. So D is the winner.
[/THINK]
D

This question illustrates the point made earlier, that minimum contacts analysis can turn (within limits) on the size of the defendant as compared to the plaintiff. Here, Mary’s contacts in California would almost certainly not support personal jurisdiction over a California defendant sued in a Massachusetts court. Nor would they support jurisdiction over a large out-of-state defendant. But it is doubtful that the Supreme Court would hold that Exxon Mobil could not obtain personal jurisdiction over Mary in California. While her contacts are minimal, they did give rise to the claim. Exxon Mobil could choose a forum that is less convenient to Mary, so long as it could fair enough to allow the case to proceed. A suggests that Mary is only subject to jurisdiction in a state if she was there for an extended stay. This isn’t so; people can be subject to jurisdiction based on very brief contacts if they give rise to the claim. For example, World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson (see Question 3) held that Seaway, a New York buyer of an Audi, was subject to jurisdiction in Oklahoma, even though she only stopped there briefly on a driving vacation. And B suggests that the court should refuse to exercise jurisdiction if it would be very inconvenient to the defendant to appear and defend the case. But the focus of the analysis must be on the defendant’s contacts, not on the defendant’s resources. If the defendant has established minimum contacts in the state, the court will usually exercise jurisdiction, even if it is less convenient for the defendant to return and defend the action there. C is an interesting choice. It suggests that Exxon Mobil, though it initiated the suit in California, could be forced to litigate in Massachusetts, because it would be very inconvenient for Mary to defend in California. This is an interesting suggestion, but it hasn’t been accepted by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court has never required a plaintiff to choose the most convenient forum, even if the defendant is an individual with limited resources. The focus of the analysis is on the defendant’s contacts, not on the relative convenience of the parties. If the defendant has minimum contacts in the state, the court will usually exercise jurisdiction, even if it is less convenient for the defendant to return and defend the action there. So D is the best answer. It would not be fair to bar Exxon Mobil’s claim because Mary would find it extremely inconvenient to return and defend the action in California. The Supreme Court has never suggested that a defendant’s resources are relevant to the minimum contacts analysis. If they were, a small defendant would always argue that the plaintiff should litigate in the plaintiff’s home state, on the ground that it would be too burdensome to travel to the forum state. This might put the plaintiff’s claim, or the defendant’s defense, beyond the reach of the court. So, while D is a hard result for Mary, it is likely the law.
[/THINK]
D

[THINK]
This is a tough case. It pushes personal jurisdiction analysis to the limits. D is wrong, because Dispos-All has not sent its product into Maryland. It has disposed of waste in Delaware, but that is not the same thing as selling a product and having it taken to another state. A is also wrong. This is not a stream-of-commerce case, because Dispos-All has not placed a product into the stream of commerce and the product has not been taken to Maryland by a third party. Dispos-All has disposed of waste in Delaware, and the waste has migrated to Maryland because of Dispos-All’s negligent employee. B is wrong too, because Dispos-All has reached into Maryland to cause an event—pollution in Maryland—that it could foresee would take place in Maryland. It can’t argue, ‘‘We didn’t intend to pollute in Maryland, so we aren’t subject to personal jurisdiction there.’’ If that were a complete defense, manufacturers could pollute at will, as long as they were careful not to pollute in the state where they are sued. They would simply have to argue, ‘‘We only polluted in Utah, so we aren’t subject to personal jurisdiction in Idaho.’’ Pollution doesn’t recognize state lines, and a polluter can’t limit its exposure to personal jurisdiction in states where its pollution causes damage by arguing that it only intended to pollute in the state where it disposed of the waste. It subjecting itself to jurisdiction in states where it could foresee that its acts would cause adverse effects. Here, Dispos-All could foresee that negligent disposal at its landfill might lead to pollution in Maryland, since it knew that the groundwater ran from the landfill toward the Maryland aquifer. C rules.
[/THINK]
C

[THINK]
The suggestion in Shaffer v. Heitner that all assertions of jurisdiction must meet the standards of International Shoe, 326 U.S. 310, has radically changed the law of in rem and quasi in rem jurisdiction. If it means what it says, it would bar many traditional exercises of quasi in rem jurisdiction, including the case that was before the Court in Shaffer. If the Court’s broad language in Shaffer is to be taken at face value, E is the proper answer. None of the cases is proper after Shaffer, because in each the plaintiff seeks to assert jurisdiction over an unrelated claim by seizing property of the defendant. In A, Ohora’s claim arises out of her injury on the real estate. But she doesn’t claim any preexisting interest in it that entitles her to its sale. Rather, she invokes the court’s power to seize Roux’s property as an indirect way of requiring Roux to defend the personal injury action in Nebraska. This is quasi in rem jurisdiction, very type II. In B, Ohora’s claim is to establish her exclusive right to the farm. She could do this by suing Roux directly for a judgment establishing that she alone owns the farm. But that might not be possible if Roux is a citizen of another state and there is no basis for personal jurisdiction over him there. Instead, Ohora uses an in rem procedure to assert jurisdiction over Roux based on his interest in the Nebraska farm. This is an exercise of quasi in rem jurisdiction, because Ohora’s claim is not against the farm itself, but against Roux personally, and the farm is only an asset seized to provide the court a basis for requiring Roux to defend. True, Ohora’s claim does affect the farm, by establishing her exclusive right to it, but it is not a claim ‘‘about the farm’’ (as in Gitlin v. Levine, 571 N.E.2d 1062 (Ill. App. Ct. 1991)), but a claim against Roux that will be satisfied by the sale of the farm. C is also a type II quasi in rem case. Consolidated’s claim is against Roux for the installment payments. It could sue Roux directly on that claim in any state where there is a basis for exercising personal jurisdiction over him. But if no such basis exists, it can still sue in Nebraska, by seizing an asset of Roux’s located in Nebraska. The asset attached here, the crane, is unrelated to Ohora’s claim. It was sold to Roux in Iowa, not Nebraska. But under traditional attachment practice, any asset of the defendant located in the state could be seized to provide a basis for the court to exercise jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. If Shaffer means what it says, this can no longer be done.
[/THINK]
E

[THINK]
This question is really pretty droll. D is right, because none of the other statements is true. Shaffer did not declare the exercise of all three types of in rem jurisdiction unconstitutional. It left traditional in rem jurisdiction, based on attachment of property by the court, unchanged. It did not expressly pronounce on the constitutionality of type I quasi in rem jurisdiction, but probably left it intact as well. Shaffer based its opinion on the logic of type II quasi in rem jurisdiction, that is, the practice of hanging a claim against a defendant that is unrelated to the property attached simply because the defendant owns property in the state. Shaffer rejected this type of quasi in rem jurisdiction, but said nothing about the other two. So A and B are both wrong. C, however, is right, because Shaffer did hold that type II quasi in rem jurisdiction is unconstitutional. Natch, D is the right answer.
[/THINK]
D

The real meaning of ‘‘our long-arm statute goes to the limits of due process’’ is a mystery in many states. If Acadia interprets its statute to authorize all jurisdiction that is constitutionally permissible, A is right. But it seems doubtful that the Acadia court would ascribe that meaning to the statute. If it did, why would it need to write that the statute ‘‘goes to the limits of due process’’? Why not just say, ‘‘we can exercise jurisdiction if it is constitutionally permissible?’’ More likely, the Acadia court means that it will construe the long-arm statute to reach as far as it constitutionally can. That is, it will assume that each section of the statute is valid, and will be construed to reach as far as the Due Process Clause allows. This is what the Acadia court would likely do if it took the position that it ‘‘can’t be that our legislature has authorized jurisdiction that is beyond constitutional bounds.’’ If that is what the Acadia court means by ‘‘going to the limits of due process,’’ B is the right answer. The court would likely conclude that the statute authorizes jurisdiction here, by construing the ‘‘personal injury’’ section to reach Margules’s claim. Margules did cause a personal injury to Perrone in Acadia, even if he did it by long-distance phone call. Surely, the Acadia court could require Margules to defend this claim in Acadia. Perrone is a resident of the state; the claim arises from a job opportunity in Acadia. Margules has deliberately interfered with that opportunity, and caused Perrone injury in Acadia. It would not be unreasonable for the Acadia court to require Margules to come and defend this claim in Acadia. Thus, the ‘‘personal injury’’ section of the long-arm statute reaches to the limits of due process, and the Acadia court is likely to so hold. C is wrong, because it implies that the court would likely hold that the statute does not authorize jurisdiction, but that it would be constitutional to exercise it. This is almost certainly not the interpretation the Acadia court would give the statute, if it has held that it ‘‘goes to the limits of due process.’’ D is also wrong, because the Acadia court is not likely to hold that it would exceed due process limits to exercise jurisdiction over Margules for this claim. As just discussed, it very likely would be within constitutional bounds to exercise jurisdiction over Margules for this claim. The fact that the defendant’s act that gave rise to the claim took place in another state has never been dispositive of the purposeful availment analysis. In World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286 (1980), the Supreme Court upheld jurisdiction over a driver from New York who bought her Audi in New York from a New York dealer, where a passenger from New York was injured in Oklahoma when the car, driven by the buyer, collided with another car in Oklahoma. Here, the effect of Margules’s call will be felt primarily in Acadia, and the call was deliberately aimed at Acadia. This is very similar to Calder v. Jones, 465 U.S. 783 (1984), in which the Supreme Court upheld jurisdiction over Florida defendants who wrote an allegedly defamatory article about a California actress for a California magazine. Margules has deliberately reached into Acadia to cause a substantial adverse effect on Perrone in Acadia. This is a contact that should support personal jurisdiction over Margules for this claim.
[/THINK]
B

[THINK]
In this case Ausable, a corporation from another state, has not entered Tennessee itself to do business. Instead, it has entered into a contractual arrangement with a distributor in Kentucky, and has authorized that distributor to resell its products in several states, including Tennessee. The question is whether this can support personal jurisdiction over Ausable itself for a claim that arises from the sale of a motor covered by the distributorship contract. It should be clear that Ausable has not directly engaged in a purposeful transaction of business in Tennessee that gives rise to Lemmon’s claim. It hasn’t been there at all. It has simply contracted with a distributor in Kentucky, and authorized Sunday River to resell its products in several states. Sunday River has taken twelve of those motors into Tennessee and resold them there. The question is whether, given the broad ‘‘goes to the limits of due process’’ approach to long-arm interpretation, the Tennessee court would conclude that Ausable itself has ‘‘transacted business’’ in Tennessee, so as to satisfy the long-arm statute. I think not. A is wrong, because the Tennessee court is unlikely to conclude that Ausable itself has transacted business in Tennessee, so as to satisfy the long-arm statute. While Ausable has authorized Sunday River to resell its products in Tennessee, and even required it to sell a certain volume there, that doesn’t mean that Ausable itself has transacted business in Tennessee. If we equated Ausable’s actions with those of its distributor, we would essentially be treating Ausable and Sunday River as a single entity, which they clearly are not. Sunday River is an independent reseller, and in reselling the motors it buys from Ausable, it acts as Sunday River’s agent for sale, not as Ausable’s. Thus, while Sunday River’s sales in Tennessee would likely support personal jurisdiction over Sunday River (if, say, Lemmon sued it for co-liability for the injury), it would be going too far to treat those sales as a transaction of business by Ausable itself. Thus, the court would likely conclude that Ausable has not itself transacted business in Tennessee, so that the long-arm statute does not reach to jurisdiction over it. B is the best answer here. The case will likely be dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction, because Ausable’s actions do not satisfy the long-arm statute. The court need not reach the due process question, since it has no statutory authority to hear the case. The ‘‘goes to the limits of due process’’ approach doesn’t mean that the court will always take jurisdiction if it can. It means that the court will read the long-arm statute as broadly as it can, so that, for example, if the long-arm statute is ambiguous as to whether it applies to a particular case, the court will usually construe it to reach the case, so long as doing so would not exceed due process constraints. But this does not mean that the statute will be stretched to the breaking point to reach a defendant. If the statute clearly does not apply, the court will dismiss, whether or not it would be constitutionally permissible to exercise jurisdiction over the defendant. Here, the long-arm statute clearly does not reach Ausable’s claim, since Ausable has not itself transacted business in the state. C is also wrong, because it would not exceed due process limits for Tennessee to exercise jurisdiction over Ausable. It would not be unfair, in light of Ausable’s decision to distribute its motors in Tennessee, to allow it to anticipate lawsuits from Tennessee buyers in Tennessee courts. Indeed, one might argue that it would be unreasonable for Ausable to allow resale of its products into Tennessee, but to disclaim an affinity for the state that would support personal jurisdiction for claims arising from those sales. While Ausable has not entered Tennessee, it has affirmatively sought to profit from sales in Tennessee, and could foresee that its products would give rise to claims there. It would not be unreasonable for the Tennessee court to exercise jurisdiction over it for such a claim. But since the long-arm statute does not authorize jurisdiction over Ausable, the case will be dismissed.
[/THINK]
B

This question explores the relation between a direct defense of a suit in the rendering court and a collateral attack on the judgment in another. The facts here are a bit different from Chief Judge Kozinski’s hypothetical, but the point is the same: Can a defendant who appears specially in the rendering court, loses on the jurisdiction question, and then defaults, resist enforcement of the resulting default judgment when the plaintiff brings it to the enforcing court? The answer, once again, is no. B is right. Once Ito appeared specially in the Emporia court and lost on the objection to personal jurisdiction, the court had the power to proceed with the case. When it entered the default judgment for Ervin, that judgment is presumptively valid, even if the court that rendered it made a mistake about its power to hear the case. When Ervin brings it to Acadia to enforce, the Acadia court will not allow Ito to relitigate the issue of whether the Emporia court had jurisdiction over him. It will assume that the Emporia court did, since it was there to decide that question, and Ito, having lost on it in the Emporia trial court, has not taken an appeal. At this point, the validity of the Emporia judgment is res judicata on the issue of jurisdiction, and Ito will not be allowed to relitigate it in the Acadia action. A is wrong, because the Acadia court will not hear an appeal from the Emporia judgment. The issue here is not whether the Emporia judgment is valid. That question is beyond the power of the Acadia court to decide. The only question the Acadia court can decide is whether it is barred from enforcing the judgment on the grounds Ito offers. And it is not barred, because Ito has not properly preserved the issue of the Emporia court’s lack of jurisdiction. He could have taken an appeal in Emporia after the trial court rejected his special appearance objection, but he chose not to. C is wrong, because, having defaulted on the merits in Emporia, it is irrelevant that Ito made a proper pre- judgment objection to personal jurisdiction in that court. He has lost the chance to litigate the merits in Emporia, and the price of that choice is that he will be precluded from resisting enforcement of the Emporia judgment in another state on the ground that the Emporia court lacked personal jurisdiction over him.
[/THINK]
B

[THINK]
This question explores the options if the enforcing court determines that it lacks personal jurisdiction over the defendant. The problem indicates that the court will likely conclude that it lacks personal jurisdiction over Ito for the underlying fraud claim, since it arises out of Acadia and Ito has no contact in New Mexico that gave rise to the claim. He does have minimum contacts with New Mexico, but contacts that arise from them, such as owning a time share, that do not give rise to the claim are insufficient to support personal jurisdiction.
